area.name: Burbank, California
area.summary: Burbank grew from Dr. David Burbank's sheep ranch on two Mexican-era ranchos into a town founded in 1887, then a farm, wine and rail community. Trucks, aircraft and film and TV studios made it industrial and famous. Downtown still holds a 1937 post office, a 1943 City Hall and the ghost of the Golden Mall.
keyPoints: Two ranchos, Spanish-era San Rafael and Mexican-era La Providencia, were merged into one sheep ranch by dentist David Burbank in 1867.
The 1887 land boom created the town; its Southern Pacific depot and Olive Avenue spine still organise downtown.
Farms, vineyards and a branch railroad came first; Moreland trucks (1917), Lockheed (1928) and the studios turned Burbank industrial.
Downtown reinvented itself: the pedestrian Golden Mall (1967-89) gave way to Burbank Town Center (1991).

timeline.text: Spanish padres plant four sycamores as a landmark midway between the missions (per city marker).
Rancho La Providencia granted to Vicente de la Ossa.
Battle of Providencia: Californio rebels face down Governor Micheltorena's troops.
Dr. David Burbank buys about 9,200 acres of the two ranchos for about $9,000 and runs sheep.
Providencia Land, Water and Development Co. opens the townsite; Southern Pacific depot completed.
City raises $25,000 for land to lure Moreland Truck Co. to San Fernando Rd. at Alameda.

trivia: Burbank once had many wineries; the last, Brusso Winery near the airport, ran until about 1967.
The Burbank Historical Society's museum claims to be among the largest of any US local history society by floor area.

places.name: Burbank City Hall
places.located: App position (Wikidata); HMDB's marker coordinate at 275 E. Olive Ave (34.1819, -118.3078) agrees within about 100 ft.
places.summary: Streamline Moderne civic landmark designed by William Allen and George W. Lutzi, built by city employees and finished in 1943; listed on the National Register in 1996.
places.seeToday: The Art Deco/Moderne building at Olive Ave. and 3rd St. with an HMDB plaque; film crews often borrow it.
keyPoints: Designed by William Allen and George W. Lutzi; built by city employees in 1943.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places on April 18, 1996.
HMDB's transcription of the lobby signs includes a profile of muralist Hugo Ballin.
HMDB files it under Art Deco and WPA projects.

timeline.text: Burbank's first City Hall opens across the street.

trivia: Wikipedia cites city officials saying film companies request to use City Hall constantly (used only to check facts).

sources.title: City of Burbank: Historic Properties list

places.name: Burbank Downtown Post Office
places.localName: United States Post Office, Burbank Downtown Station
places.located: App position (Wikidata); HMDB marker gives 34.1804, -118.3094 at 135 E. Olive Ave (the NPS lists 125 E. Olive).
places.summary: A 1937 federal post office, Burbank's first National Register listing (1985), still working as the downtown station.
places.seeToday: A working post office on Olive Ave. with an HMDB National Register plaque.
keyPoints: Built in 1937; listed January 11, 1985 (NRIS 85000127) for architecture.
Part of the multiple listing 'US Post Offices in California 1900-1941'.
A 1938 newspaper headline noted cornerstone rites would be omitted.
Absorbed the closed Glenoaks Post Office in 2014.

timeline.text: Evening Citizen News reports cornerstone rites omitted.
Glenoaks Post Office closes; functions move here.

trivia: Wikipedia notes that when City Hall was listed in 1996 it became Burbank's second listed building, after this post office.

sources.title: NPS NRHP: US Post Office, Burbank Downtown Station

places.name: Site of Burbank's First City Hall
places.located: Approximate: HMDB gives the address 250 E. Olive Ave and says the marker is within shouting distance of City Hall; coordinates are my estimate.
places.summary: A small plaque records that Burbank's first City Hall was built here in 1916, five years after the city incorporated.
places.seeToday: A Heritage Commission plaque on Olive Ave.; the 1916 building itself is gone.
keyPoints: Plaque text: first City Hall built here in 1916.
Erected by the Burbank Heritage Commission and the Cusumano family.
Burbank incorporated in 1911.

timeline.text: Replaced by the current City Hall.

trivia: A nearby HMDB marker for Cartoon Network Studios is recorded as confirmed missing.

places.name: Story Hardware
places.located: HMDB coordinate 34°10.834′N 118°18.487′W; the plaque's address is on S. San Fernando Blvd. (sources say 130, 140 or 150), so treat as roughly ±300 ft.
places.summary: Site where pioneer Thomas Story opened Story & Sons Hardware in 1915; the shop lasted until 1986.
places.seeToday: A plaque on San Fernando Blvd. just south of Olive Ave.; the store is gone.
keyPoints: Thomas Story arrived in 1877 and opened Burbank's first livery stable in 1899.
He became first President of the Board of Trustees (mayor equivalent) at incorporation in 1911.
Story died in 1937; the hardware store kept operating until 1986.

timeline.text: Becomes first Board of Trustees president.

trivia: Open Plaques lists the same plaque at 130 San Fernando Blvd.

places.name: Time Capsules and the Central Library site
places.located: HMDB coordinate 34°11.018′N 118°18.366′W; marker in the park beside the Central Library at 418 E. Olive Ave.
places.summary: Marker for city time capsules sealed in the 1970s, beside the library site where an older 1937 capsule was damaged and finally opened in 1986.
places.seeToday: A monument in the park next to the Central Library at Olive Ave. and Glenoaks Blvd.
keyPoints: HMDB: capsules sealed July 4, 1977 by the Bicentennial Committee; LAist says the original was placed in 1976.
When the 2001 monument was opened it was empty and held the original capsule instead.
A 1937 capsule from the old library cornerstone was damaged in demolition and opened at City Hall in 1986.
A new Central Library is expected in 2029, per HMDB.

timeline.text: Capsule sealed in the old library cornerstone.

trivia: The 1986 opening was widely seen as a letdown: mostly library receipts.

sources.title: HMDB: City of Burbank Time Capsules

places.name: Downtown Burbank Station (old Southern Pacific depot)
places.kind: Rail station and former depot site
places.located: App position (Wikidata). Sources found don't give the old depot's exact footprint, only that today's station sits under the Olive Ave. bridge.
places.summary: Burbank's rail link since the Southern Pacific depot of 1887; a horsecar line once ran from it to Sunset Canyon.
places.seeToday: A modern station beneath the Olive Ave. bridge; HMDB lists a 'Burbank Railway Depot' marker nearby that I couldn't read.
keyPoints: A Southern Pacific depot was completed in 1887 (Wikipedia, used as a check).
An 1889 photo shows horsecar tracks from the SP station to Sunset Canyon.
The Olive Ave. bridge over the SP tracks opened August 12, 1958.
myBurbank contrasts the old depot photos with today's station.

timeline.text: Horsecar line runs station to Sunset Canyon.

trivia: Burbank in Focus has a 1980s photo captioned 'Old Burbank Train Station'.

places.name: Golden Mall
places.located: App position; Wikipedia gives 34.1808, -118.3109. The mall was a stretch of San Fernando Blvd., not a single spot.
places.summary: San Fernando Boulevard was closed to cars in November 1967 for a $915,000 pedestrian mall; it faded and cars returned from 1987.
places.seeToday: Ordinary shops and cafés along San Fernando Blvd. (now 'Burbank Village'); little mall infrastructure remains.
keyPoints: Opened November 1967, cost $915,000.
A 1985 plan to reopen it to traffic led to the first blocks reopening in 1987.
Revitalisation shifted to the empty 40-acre lot that became Burbank Town Center.
Pedestrian mall era ended in 1989.
trivia: Early anchors included JCPenney, per a Los Angeles real estate blog.

places.name: Burbank Town Center
places.kind: Shopping centre on a redevelopment site
places.located: App position; Wikipedia gives 34.1837, -118.3126 (201 E. Magnolia Blvd.).
places.summary: Opened August 21, 1991 as Media City Center on a vacant 40-acre redevelopment parcel beside the old Golden Mall.
places.seeToday: A multi-level mall at 201 E. Magnolia Blvd.; IKEA, its first store, left in 2017.
keyPoints: Developer Alexander Haagen; opened August 21, 1991.
IKEA opened first, in 1990, on a 99-year city lease signed in 1989.
IKEA closed February 4, 2017 for a bigger store nearby.
A county museum branch was planned but delayed.

timeline.text: Photos show the vacant Town Center site.

trivia: The first name was Media City Center.

sources.title: Burbank in Focus: Future site photos

places.name: The Burbank Building corner (Olive Ave. and San Fernando Rd.)
places.located: Approximate: sources name only the corner (northeast corner of Olive and San Fernando). I placed it near the Golden Mall point.
places.summary: Burbank's first brick building stood at this corner in the boom years; a 1908 bank and 1910 street scenes show the intersection as the town's centre.
places.seeToday: Nothing marks the spot; today it is a downtown intersection.
keyPoints: Calisphere describes the first brick building on the northeast corner.
A c.1890 photo of 'the Burbank Building' is the cover of the book Lost Burbank.
Burbank State Bank, the first bank, opened in 1908 near here.
A c.1910 USC photograph shows San Fernando Blvd. at Olive.
trivia: Dr. Burbank and his son built the Burbank Villa on Olive Ave. near today's First Street.

sources.title: Burbank in Focus: Burbank State Bank
Calisphere: San Fernando Blvd. at Olive, c.1910

places.name: Compass Tree Park
places.located: HMDB coordinate 34°10.296′N 118°18.55′W; marker at Lake St. and Providencia Ave. (621 S. Lake St.).
places.summary: A 2002 city marker says Spanish padres planted four sycamores in 1817 as a compass-point landmark between the missions.
places.seeToday: A small park with a marker; the original trees were removed in the 1940s.
keyPoints: Per the marker, four trees were planted in 1817 about midway between the Los Angeles and San Fernando missions.
They grew over 100 ft and marked the four compass directions.
Settlers later danced on a cement platform around them.
The park honours early Spanish heritage.
trivia: The 1817 date is the marker's claim; I found no independent source.

places.name: Mentzer House and Gordon R. Howard Museum
places.localName: Mentzer House / Gordon R. Howard Museum
places.kind: Boom-era house and local history museum
places.located: Approximate: addresses 115 N. Lomita St. and 1100 W. Clark Ave. in George Izay Park; coordinates estimated from the nearby F-104 marker.
places.summary: An 1887 boom-town house, moved to Olive Ave. in 1977, fronting the volunteer-run museum of the Burbank Historical Society.
places.seeToday: The restored Victorian on Olive Ave. leads into a 20,000 sq ft museum. Hours are limited, so check the society's site.
keyPoints: Built in 1887 by the Providencia Land, Water and Development Co.; only six of 30 planned houses were completed.
Moved from near Palm Ave. and 6th St. to 321 E. Orange Grove about 1920, then to Olive Ave. in 1977.
The historical society was founded in 1973; the museum opened in 1983.
Run entirely by volunteers, separate from the city.
trivia: Called the last remaining 'boom house' from the 1880s land boom by one local outlet.

sources.title: Atlas Obscura: Gordon R. Howard Museum
Toluca Lake: History close to home

places.name: 'Spirit of Burbank' F-104 Starfighter
places.located: HMDB coordinate 34°10.328′N 118°19.104′W at the Olive Recreation Center, George Izay Park (1111 W. Olive Ave.).
places.summary: A restored Lockheed F-104D jet saluting Lockheed's Burbank workforce, placed in 1984-85.
places.seeToday: A blue-and-white jet on a pedestal with a plaque and a small time-capsule monument.
keyPoints: F-104 was designed by Kelly Johnson's Skunk Works in Burbank, the first Mach 2 production jet.
Tail 57-1334, an F-104D built in 1957; restored by Lockheed staff in 1984.
Mayor Daniel Remy led the 1984 tribute to Lockheed.
A 1994 capsule marks 66 years of Lockheed in Burbank.
trivia: The city ran a monument restoration project in recent years.

places.name: Burbank Branch Railroad sculpture
places.located: HMDB/HMP coordinate 34°10.762′N 118°19.475′W; marker text itself was only partly readable.
places.summary: A marker and sculpture with original track recall the branch line that carried local melons, fruit and grapes.
places.seeToday: A sculpture using a section of original rail with spikes and crossties.
keyPoints: The line let farmers ship melons, citrus, peaches and grapes.
Marker text says the Chandler Blvd. line stayed in service for years.
The sculpture uses real track and spikes.

timeline.text: Branch line opens (year not in the marker text I could read).

trivia: HMDB measures it about 0.9 mi from the post office.

sources.title: Historical Marker Project: Burbank Branch Railroad

places.name: Sunset Canyon Country Club Gate
places.located: HMDB coordinate 34°11.554′N 118°17.791′W at Country Club Dr. and Sunset Canyon Dr.
places.summary: Gate marking the 1921 nine-hole Sunset Canyon Country Club, whose 1920s clubhouse is now a church.
places.seeToday: A Heritage Commission marker at the canyon mouth; the later clubhouse is now an LDS church.
keyPoints: Opened in 1921 as a private nine-hole course.
The first clubhouse stood hundreds of yards up the canyon.
A new clubhouse (1926-27) is now a church at 136 N. Sunset Canyon Dr.
Erected in 2001 by the Burbank Heritage Commission.
trivia: Burbank in Focus dates the clubhouse 1926; the marker says 1927.

sources.title: HMDB: Sunset Canyon Country Club Gate
Burbank in Focus: Sunset Canyon Country Club

places.name: Burbank High School
places.located: App position; school address 902 N. Third St. The 1910 and 1922 buildings stood elsewhere.
places.summary: Burbank left Glendale's high school district in 1908; its 1910 Union High building and a 1922 campus on this side of town are gone.
places.seeToday: A modern campus rebuilt from 2003; nothing of the 1922 school remains.
keyPoints: Burbank formed its own high school district in 1908.
The first building opened in September 1910 at Cypress and San Fernando Blvd.
The 1921-22 building stood between 3rd and 4th Streets and was demolished in 2002.
Burbank bid to host the UC Southern Branch in 1925.
trivia: The film Corvette Summer shot in its auto shop and classrooms.

sources.title: BHS Class of '67: History of Burbank High
Burbank in Focus: rememBURBANK, UC Burbank (1925)

places.name: St. Robert Bellarmine Catholic Church
places.located: App position; parish address 133 N. 5th St.
places.summary: Parish founded in 1907 as Holy Trinity, rebuilt in the 1930s in a colonial-American style by Msgr. Martin Keating.
places.seeToday: A campus modelled on Monticello, Independence Hall and Mount Vernon.
keyPoints: Founded in 1907, one of the San Fernando Valley's first Catholic parishes.
Renamed in 1939 for St. Robert Bellarmine.
School founded in 1936; Msgr. Keating pastor 1930-1967.
Mother Cabrini obtained land in the Verdugo foothills nearby.
trivia: Mother Cabrini attended Mass at Holy Trinity while in Burbank.

places.name: Bellarmine-Jefferson High School (and the first Central Library)
places.located: App position and Wikipedia coordinate; 465 E. Olive Ave.
places.summary: Catholic high school founded in 1944 and closed in 2018, built partly where Burbank's Spanish-style first permanent library stood.
places.seeToday: A closed campus on Olive Ave.
keyPoints: Founded by Msgr. Martin Keating in 1944; named for Robert Bellarmine and Thomas Jefferson.
Closed 2018.
A Spanish-style library once stood where part of the campus ends.
The 1937 library capsule was buried in that library's cornerstone.
trivia: The Jefferson link reflects Keating's belief that Bellarmine influenced the Declaration.

sources.title: Burbank in Focus: B-J High School

places.name: St. John Paul II STEM Academy
places.localName: St. John Paul II STEM Academy
places.located: Same campus as Bellarmine-Jefferson (465 E. Olive Ave.).
places.summary: A Catholic STEM high school that reopened the old Bellarmine-Jefferson campus in August 2019 and closed in June 2020.
places.seeToday: Same closed campus.
keyPoints: Launched August 2019 with a freshman class.
Closed June 2020 after one year.
Run by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles.
trivia: Lasted one school year.

sources.title: Burbank in Focus: B-J High School

places.name: Burbank Western Channel
places.located: App position; the channel is a 6.3-mile line, so this is one point on it.
places.summary: A concrete wash carrying runoff through downtown to the Los Angeles River; channelising followed the 1938 flood.
places.seeToday: A fenced concrete channel beside I-5.
keyPoints: 6.3-mile concrete channel through downtown Burbank.
It joins the LA River by the Equestrian Center.
The March 1938 flood led to the channel network.
A 1938 photo shows flooding near Niagara St.
trivia: The LA River changes channel shape after receiving this wash.

places.name: Rancho Cahuenga
places.located: Approximate: app position; boundaries not mapped in sources found. Wikipedia says the LA River channel runs through it.
places.summary: A 388-acre inholding inside Rancho Providencia; David Burbank acquired it in 1867.
places.seeToday: Nothing marks it.
keyPoints: Inside the Rancho Providencia grant.
Traded in 1845 for Rancho Tujunga.
Sold to David Burbank in 1867.
Not the same as Campo de Cahuenga in Studio City.
trivia: Often confused with Campo de Cahuenga.

places.name: Site of the Battle of Providencia (1845)
places.located: Low: sources disagree. Wikipedia's pin is 34.180, -118.328; Crescenta Valley Weekly places it near the Equestrian Center; an Army museum text says west of Cahuenga Pass.
places.summary: On February 19-20, 1845, Californio rebels faced down Governor Micheltorena's troops on Rancho Providencia in a nearly bloodless artillery duel.
places.seeToday: Nothing marks the spot.
keyPoints: Roughly 200 men per side; cannons stayed at long range.
Micheltorena was ousted; Pío Pico became governor.
Casualties reported as a horse and a mule.
Cannonballs turned up in Burbank into the 20th century.
trivia: Also called the Second Battle of Cahuenga Pass.

places.name: Former Moreland Truck Company factory site
places.located: Approximate: sources give the corner of San Fernando Rd. and Alameda Ave. (southwest corner); coordinates are my estimate.
places.summary: In 1917 Burbank raised $25,000 to give Moreland Trucks 25 acres, the city's first big factory; it closed in 1940 and was demolished around 1999.
places.seeToday: Nothing marks the spot.
keyPoints: City raised $25,000 for 25 acres at San Fernando Rd. and Alameda Ave.
Trucks carried a 'Made in Burbank' label.
Plant closed in 1940; later Vega Aircraft used buildings.
Buildings were demolished around 1999.
trivia: Exports reached Australia, South America and the Philippines.

places.name: Walt Disney Studios, Burbank (Walt's 100th marker)
places.located: HMDB coordinate 34°9.495′N 118°19.564′W (2400 W. Alameda Ave.); studio not open to the public.
places.summary: Disney's Burbank lot carries a 2001 marker for Walt's 100th birthday and one for nitrate film vaults built in 1939.
places.seeToday: Gates at Alameda Ave. and Buena Vista St.; markers are inside the lot.
keyPoints: Marker dated December 5, 2001, signed by Michael Eisner and Roy E. Disney.
About 15 markers cluster here.
Nitrate Film Vaults built 1939, used until 2014.
1990s construction of the Animation building.
trivia: The marker's key line says it began with a man, not a mouse.

places.name: McCambridge Park and the Moving Wall memorial
places.located: Approximate: HMDB gives the address 1320 N. San Fernando Blvd., about a mile from City Hall; coordinates are my estimate.
places.summary: A stone marks where the Vietnam Moving Wall stood in 1998; the park is also Burbank's annual Memorial Day site.
places.seeToday: A memorial stone in the park's corner.
keyPoints: The Moving Wall visited February 16-22, 1998.
The stone was dedicated on Veterans Day 1998.
Park named for James H. McCambridge in 1953.
Annual Memorial Day ceremony with a rose for each name.
trivia: Wall is half-size, devised by John Devitt.

places.name: UT Los Angeles Center
places.located: App position only; I couldn't find a street address.
places.summary: The University of Texas at Austin's Semester in Los Angeles programme, founded in 2005.
places.seeToday: Likely an ordinary downtown building.
keyPoints: Founded 2005 with $500,000 from the Cain Foundation.
First permanent UT campus outside Texas.
Moved to a new facility in 2017.
trivia: One of few entertainment-focused programmes run by an out-of-state university.
